主要内容: The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the median number of years wage and salary workers had been with their current employer was 4.6 in January 2012, up from 4.4 years in January 2010. This data comes from the Current Population Survey (CPS), which collects information on employee tenure every two years since 1996. The CPS is a monthly survey of about 60,000 households, providing insights into the labor force status of the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over. Factors such as changes in the age profile of workers, the number of hires, and separations can influence median tenure. For instance, older workers tend to have longer tenure, with those aged 65 and over having a median tenure of 10.3 years, compared to 3.2 years for workers aged 25 to 34. In the public sector, the median tenure was 7.8 years, nearly double that of the private sector (4.2 years). Manufacturing workers had the highest median tenure (6.0 years), while those in leisure and hospitality had the lowest (2.4 years). In January 2012, workers in management, professional, and related occupations had the highest median tenure (5.5 years) among major occupational groups. Within this group, employees in architecture and engineering occupations had the longest tenure at 7.0 years, followed by management occupations at 6.3 years. In contrast, workers in service occupations, who are generally younger, had the lowest median tenure at 3.2 years. Among service workers, food service workers had the shortest median tenure at 2.3 years. The data were collected through a supplement to the January 2012 Current Population Survey (CPS), which provides information on labor force status, demographics, and worker tenure. The CPS, conducted by the U.S. Census Bureau for the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), is a monthly survey of about 60,000 eligible households. The 2012 supplement included questions on worker displacement and tenure with current employers. The data reflect the introduction of Census 2010 population controls, which may affect comparability with prior years. The reliability of the estimates is subject to both sampling and nonsampling errors, with a 90% confidence level that estimates differ by no more than 1.6 standard errors from the true population value. The CPS data also include follow-up questions to obtain more precise information on workers with short tenure.
